The chapter on exponential functions and logarithms (6) explains things
like the one-to-one property being for solving exponential functions by
base matching, but only when the base is a positive number that is not 1
(which is correct, as far as establishing a continuous function, you don't
want negative values which would simply be disjointed 'points' for negative
integers). The problems come up later, in Geometric Sequences (13.3).

No mention within the section itself is made as to solving questions like
exercise 44 of Section 13.3:

For the following exercises, find the number of terms in the given finite
geometric sequence.

a_n = {-1, 3, -9, ..., 2187}

In this case, a student working from the book should be able to reach this
point in solving it:

-2187 = (-3)^(n-1)

The problem here is that, going by the previous definitions, the next step
of turning -2187 into -3 raised to the power of 7, and solving 7 = n-1, is
not allowed. Section 6.6 states b>0. As no exception to this rule has been
made, the solution contradicts the textbook's internal logic.

Furthermore, the fact that this question is even-numbered and the
odd-numbered question paired with it does not use the same sort of negative
means that students can't even check if they are on the right track for
this sort of thing.

What I would suggest is making a note somewhere either in the Exponents
chapter or in the Sequences chapter that it is possible to use the base
matching method, or alternatively say that when the base and resulting
value are both negative, the exponent must be an odd integer, so |-2187| =
|(-1)^(n-1)*(3)^(n-1)| which becomes 2187 = (1)(3)^(n-1).

I can't actually say that the given answer for the distance from a focus to a point on ellipse (e.g., from sun to planet) is wrong. But I think the problem should have been written differently.  It felt very strange to me (and to several of my students) the way the problem defines the angle theta.  I think it would make more sense to define theta to be the angle between the x-axis and a line drawn from the focus (sun) to the planet.  Then the line that defines the angle theta is exactly the line whose length we are finding.

By doing a limit comparison test with the p-series, you get lim as n->infinity of (ln(n)/n^a)^2 / n^p = lim as n->infinity of (ln(n))^2 / n^(2a-p).  If 2a-p is negative or zero, then the limit is infinite, so 2a-p must be positive, that is p must be less than 2a. In order for the p-series itself to converge, p must be greater than 1. The text states, "The length of this vector is also known as the scalar projection of v onto u and is denoted by [formula (2.7)]." This is misleading because the length of a vector is always nonnegative, whereas the scalar projection
comp_u v = (u dot v)/||u|| can be negative when the angle between u and v is greater than pi/2.

A more precise statement would be:
"The signed component of v in the direction of u is called the scalar projection of v onto u, and is denoted by [formula (2.7)]. Its absolute value is the length of proj_u v."

Equivalently, ||proj_u v|| = |comp_u v|.
